intro: Final Cut’s Color Wheels and Color Curves are complementary correction tools. Wheels offer broad controls for global appearance, shadows, midtones and highlights; curves let you reshape selected tonal ranges through control points. Choose the control that addresses the visible problem, and inspect the correction already on the clip before adding another.

sections.heading: Describe the correction before choosing a control
paragraphs: Identify whether the shot needs a general exposure adjustment, a tonal-region tint or a more selective contrast change. Compare the shot with its intended neighbors and keep a reference frame. A control’s name does not tell you which part of the scene should remain unchanged.

Separate an unwanted cast from intentional lighting. A warm lamp in the frame does not necessarily mean the entire image should be neutralized. Decide which skin tones, neutral objects and highlight details matter to the sequence before making a large global adjustment.

sections.heading: Inspect the native correction instances
paragraphs: Select the clip and place the playhead on a useful frame. In the Color inspector, use Add Correction to add Color Wheels or Color Curves. To modify an existing instance, select it from the Corrections list instead of adding another effect by accident.

Color Wheels provides Global, Shadows, Midtones and Highlights controls with brightness and saturation adjustments. Color Curves provides luma and color-channel curves whose control points change selected parts of the tonal response. The separate Hue/Saturation Curves effect answers a different selection problem and should not be confused with these luma and RGB curves.

sections.heading: Make a limited adjustment and compare the result
paragraphs: For a broad change, make a small wheel adjustment and watch important neutral and skin areas. For a contrast curve, establish control points deliberately and inspect how adjacent values move. A narrow intended change can affect more of the picture when a curve bends sharply.

Use the available video scopes alongside the viewer, and compare before and after at the same frame. Wheels and curves can be combined when they serve different corrections. Rename multiple correction instances to describe their purpose so a later editor can tell a contrast adjustment from a deliberate tint.

sections.heading: Verify the correction across motion and neighboring shots
paragraphs: Play the whole clip, including any lighting change. A frame that looks balanced at the start may have a different highlight or skin exposure later. Inspect gradients and fine tonal transitions for visible harshness rather than accepting a pleasing still image as proof of the complete grade.

Compare the corrected shot in sequence and export a representative interval using the project’s established color workflow. Retain the editable corrections and source. These controls cannot recover detail absent from the recording, and a more complicated curve is not evidence of greater accuracy or a better delivery file.

example: Example: a shot’s overall balance is acceptable, but its middle tones look flat. The editor tests a restrained luma curve while watching faces and highlights. They keep a separate wheel correction only if a broad tonal tint still needs adjustment, rather than stacking unexplained instances.

intro: A Final Cut library’s color-processing setting and a project’s color space answer different questions. The library establishes a processing context; the project determines the space used for its rendering and delivery. Enabling wide-gamut processing does not by itself make every source HDR or every exported movie a correct HDR deliverable.

sections.heading: Write down the source and receiving requirements
paragraphs: Identify the source’s documented color representation and the destination’s accepted delivery space. Keep camera or mastering notes with the media. A bright-looking viewer image or an HDR-looking filename is not enough to establish how the recording should be interpreted.

Record the current library and project settings before changing them. If several projects share the library, review their requirements too. A library-level adjustment made to satisfy one export can alter the context of work that another editor already approved.

sections.heading: Set the library and project deliberately
paragraphs: Select the library and open File, Library Properties, or Control-Command-J. Use Modify for Color Processing to inspect Standard or Wide Gamut HDR. Apple describes this as a library-level setting affecting processing, including aspects of log footage and effect behavior.

Inspect the particular project’s Color Space separately. HDR project choices require a wide-gamut HDR library, but the selected project space remains a separate decision. Choose it to match the intended workflow instead of assuming that the broadest available setting is always the correct delivery target.

sections.heading: Check the effect of changing the processing context
paragraphs: Compare representative clips before and after any change, especially composited titles, blended graphics and filtered footage. Apple cautions that changes to the processing context can affect their appearance. Revisit the accepted grade rather than treating a library-setting change as an invisible metadata edit.

Check source conversion as part of the chain. Mixing SDR and HDR sources calls for deliberate interpretation into the project space. Avoid adding another conversion solely because the picture differs from an old screenshot; first establish which conversion the clip already receives.

sections.heading: Verify the exported representation and appearance
paragraphs: Review the actual share settings and inspect the saved movie with a receiver appropriate to the intended space. Compare gradients, bright detail and neutral areas, not just maximum apparent brightness. Also check any SDR deliverable separately instead of assuming one file will be presented identically everywhere.

Retain the source, editable project and a note of the library, project and export choices. Changing processing space cannot reconstruct genuine highlight information that the source did not capture. SocialVidDownloader does not infer or repair a native Final Cut library’s color decisions from the finished movie.

example: Example: an editor keeps an HDR project and an SDR delivery version in a wide-gamut library. They record each project’s space and review both exports. The library’s wide-gamut setting is not used as proof that the SDR file should be labelled HDR.

intro: Before adding HDR Tools in Final Cut, inspect the clip’s Color Conform setting. Automatic Color Conform may already convert that source into the project’s color space. Apple warns that Color Conform and HDR Tools are additive; using both for the same conversion can produce an unintended double transformation.

sections.heading: Identify the conversion already taking place
paragraphs: Record the source representation and the project’s color space, including whether the HDR material is identified as HLG or PQ. Use source documentation and the clip’s interpretation rather than guessing from brightness. A wrong input assumption can make a technically successful conversion visually wrong.

Select the clip and inspect Color Conform in the Video inspector. Automatic conversion follows the source-to-project context. Manual provides an explicit Conversion Type, while None disables that Color Conform conversion. Note the current choice before changing it so the previous accepted state can be restored.

sections.heading: Choose one justified conversion path
paragraphs: Use the built-in Color Conform when it meets the workflow. Apple retains HDR Tools for compatibility and for cases needing control over the conversion’s position among other effects. Do not add HDR Tools simply because a project contains HDR material.

When the workflow calls for HDR Tools, avoid leaving a duplicate Color Conform conversion active. Choose the effect’s appropriate conversion for the actual source and destination, then inspect its position relative to other processing. Moving a transform before or after a grade changes which representation that grade receives.

sections.heading: Check the effect chain with controlled comparisons
paragraphs: Compare a representative frame and a moving interval with a known baseline. Look for compressed highlight separation, changed midtones and unexpected color shifts. If disabling one conversion corrects the picture, record the duplicate-processing diagnosis instead of hiding it with a compensating grade.

The General setting for automatic Color Conform controls its application to newly added material; it should not be treated as proof that an existing timeline has been changed throughout. Inspect the actual clips involved. Mixed-source projects can contain different settings that need separate review.

sections.heading: Verify the receiver-specific derivative
paragraphs: Export a short interval containing highlights, skin and any overlays. Inspect the file in the intended SDR or HDR receiving context and compare it with the accepted project view. Do not judge an SDR conversion solely on a display configuration meant for a different signal.

Keep the original HDR source and the editable conversion decisions. Tone mapping creates a delivery interpretation; it does not preserve every possible presentation or restore detail missing from the source. Record which transform was used and why so a later output revision does not unknowingly add the conversion again.

example: Example: an HDR clip already receives automatic conversion in an SDR project. Adding HDR Tools makes it look unexpectedly compressed. The editor checks both transformations, selects one deliberate conversion route, and verifies a new SDR export rather than pushing the grade to compensate for duplicate processing.
